newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-court to hear British boy's anti-spanking case.
newsitem.headline: Euro-court to hear British boy's anti-spanking case.

text.p: The European Commission of Human Rights agreed on Monday to take up the case of a 12-year-old British boy seeking to overturn British laws allowing his parents to smack him.

The decision is the first step towards a possible ruling by the European Court of Human Rights, which has the power to ban any type of beating of children in Britain if it agrees with his complaint. That would bring Britain into line with other European nations.

The boy's lawyers are contesting British laws sanctioning "reasonable chastisement" of children after he was beaten with a cane by his stepfather when he was nine for trying to stab his younger brother with a kitchen knife.
A court acquitted his stepfather of charges of assault.

Lawyers acting for the boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, are expected to argue the British government failed to protect the child's human rights under the European Convention of Human Rights, which bans inhuman and degrading treatment.

His natural father, with whom the boy now lives, is backing the child in the case. But his mother has defended her right to punish her son, saying he had been "totally out of control" and had "run riot" since the age of two.

Caning and other forms of corporal punishment were outlawed in British schools some years ago but courts have frequently acquitted parents who have admitted using canes, belts and electric flexes to beat their children at home.
The Commission, which announced its decision to accept the case in a statement, will now try to find a friendly settlement between the boy and the British government.
If it fails, the case will go to the European Court of Human Rights or to the 39-nation Council of Europe, which safeguards democracy and human rights. Such a process usually takes years.
Britain has sometimes lagged behind other European nations in cracking down on the use of corporal punishment.

Until 1891, for instance, British men could legally beat their wives with a stick, provided it was no thicker than a man's thumb. Under the law, husbands were also allowed to lock up their wives as a punishment.
Britain's Conservative government has criticised the rights court in a series of recent rulings that it says constitute outside meddling in its ability to govern.
London was angered last year when the court condemned Britain for the killings of three unarmed Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombers in Gibraltar in 1988.
And this year, the court condemned Britain's system for jailing minors in a ruling that could affect the sentences for two boys who battered a toddler to death in 1993.
